name: Daniel Mathalon
academic: Professor of Psychiatry · UCSF School of Medicine
bio: Daniel Mathalon is a psychiatrist and clinical neuroscientist who co-directs the Brain Imaging and EEG Laboratory with Judith Ford. He studies the brain mechanisms underlying schizophrenia and psychosis, from the clinical high-risk period through established illness. His clinical work includes caring for people who have recently developed psychosis or show early warning signs.

His research combines magnetic resonance imaging, electroencephalography, and event-related potentials to investigate brain structure, the timing of neural responses, and the organization of sensory and cognitive processing. A central goal is to improve early identification and intervention and to better understand which changes in brain function predict clinical outcomes.

Mathalon earned his BA at UC Berkeley and his PhD in Clinical Psychology at Indiana University. He completed medical school, psychiatry residency, and psychophysiology fellowship training at Stanford. His early neuroimaging work with Adolf Pfefferbaum examined how aging and head size influence brain measurements.

After research work at SRI International, he joined Yale’s faculty in 2000 and established a clinical and cognitive neuroscience laboratory. In 2007, he and Ford moved their collaboration to San Francisco and established BIEEGL at UCSF. Alongside research, he has taught medical students and psychiatry residents and mentored clinical neuroscience trainees.
summary: Psychiatrist and neuroscientist using MRI, EEG, and event-related potentials to understand schizophrenia, identify early signs of psychosis, and improve outcomes.

name: Judith Ford
academic: Professor of Psychiatry · UCSF School of Medicine
bio: Judith Ford co-directs the Brain Imaging and EEG Laboratory with Daniel Mathalon. Her research focuses on psychosis, especially auditory verbal hallucinations, and on how the brain distinguishes sensations generated by our own actions and thoughts from events in the outside world.

Ford uses neurophysiological methods to test whether difficulties predicting self-generated sensations contribute to hallucinations. When a sensation is not correctly predicted, it may be experienced as coming from an external source. Her work investigates this possibility by recording auditory-cortex responses to self-generated sounds.

This research examines sensory prediction errors and the efference-copy and corollary-discharge systems that help the brain anticipate the consequences of action. Alongside studies of vocalization, Ford has used EEG and fMRI during tasks in which people press a button to produce a sound or visual stimulus. These paradigms connect human studies of predictive coding with questions that can also be investigated in animal models.

Ford earned her BA in Psychology and her PhD in Neuroscience at Stanford, with dissertation guidance from Steven A. Hillyard at UC San Diego. After an NIH postdoctoral fellowship through UCSF, she returned to Stanford and later joined its psychiatry faculty. She moved to Yale in 2004 and established her UCSF laboratory in 2007.

Her research portfolio also includes studies of cognition after COVID-19, auditory steady-state responses, agency, and the effects of a very-low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet on neural network function in schizophrenia.
summary: Studies sensory prediction and auditory hallucinations, using EEG and fMRI to understand how the brain distinguishes self-generated sensations from external events.
projects: Neural and cognitive consequences of COVID-19 survival
Ketogenic diet and neural network instability in schizophrenia

name: Susanna Fryer
academic: Associate Professor of Psychiatry · UCSF School of Medicine
bio: Susanna Fryer is a clinical psychologist and Associate Professor in the UCSF Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences. Her research connects brain function, cognition, and behavior, with particular interests in motivation, reward processing, self-regulation, and vulnerability to mental illness.

Using neuroimaging, EEG, and neuropsychological methods, Fryer studies the cognitive features and brain differences associated with risk for psychopathology and the mechanisms through which behavioral interventions may help. Her research spans schizophrenia, depression, and related questions about emotional and attentional regulation.

Fryer completed her undergraduate work in Human Biology at Stanford, where an honors research experience sparked her interest in clinical neuroscience. She earned her PhD through the SDSU/UC San Diego Joint Doctoral Program in Clinical Psychology, specializing in neuropsychology, and completed her clinical internship at the San Francisco VA Medical Center.

Her clinical background includes cognitive-behavioral therapy and mindfulness-based approaches. She has supervised psychology trainees and provided these treatments in the San Francisco VA’s general psychiatry service. Her research has been supported by the NIH and the VA.
Outside the lab, she enjoys yoga, cooking, and crafting.
summary: Clinical psychologist studying reward processing, motivation, and self-regulation with EEG, MRI, and neuropsychological methods.
education: SDSU/UC San Diego Joint Doctoral Program
projects: Electrophysiology and non-invasive brain stimulation in depression
Multimodal neural investigation of reward processing in schizophrenia

name: Samantha Abram
bio: Samantha Abram is a clinical psychologist whose research examines motivation, decision-making, and goal-directed behavior in people with psychotic-spectrum disorders. She combines behavioral tasks and neuroscience methods to study why initiating and sustaining goals can be difficult in severe mental illness.

Her research includes EEG studies of reward processing and memory in schizophrenia, as well as work on sensory prediction and brain connectivity. She earned her PhD in Clinical Psychology at the University of Minnesota and completed clinical internship and advanced fellowship training at the San Francisco VA and UCSF.
summary: Studies motivation, reward, memory, and goal-directed behavior in psychotic-spectrum disorders using behavioral and neuroscience methods.
education: Advanced fellowship in mental illness research and treatment

name: Michael Jacob
bio: Michael Jacob is a psychiatrist and neuroscientist investigating how electrical brain activity relates to blood-flow and metabolic signals in schizophrenia. His work uses simultaneous EEG and fMRI, alongside cardiovascular measurements, to study communication between the heart and brain.

His research interests include neurometabolic coupling, embodied cognition, and the psychobiology of psychotherapy. He trained in neurobiology and anatomy and medicine at the University of Rochester, followed by psychiatry residency at UCSF and psychiatric research fellowship training at the San Francisco VA.
summary: Investigates electrical, vascular, and metabolic brain signals in schizophrenia using simultaneous EEG-fMRI and physiological measurements.

name: Jessica Hua
bio: Jessica Hua studies the mechanisms underlying schizophrenia and the development and persistence of psychosis. Her research combines neuroimaging, behavioral measures, and physiological recordings across the illness course, from clinical high risk to more established illness.

Her interests include EEG, MRI, neural plasticity, and brain stimulation. Her long-term research goals include improving prediction of psychosis risk and informing interventions grounded in an understanding of brain mechanisms. She earned her PhD in Clinical Psychology at the University of Missouri and completed postdoctoral training at the San Francisco VA and UCSF.
summary: Combines neuroimaging, behavioral measures, and electrophysiology to investigate psychosis risk, neural plasticity, and schizophrenia.

name: Maria Kryza-Lacombe
bio: Maria Kryza-Lacombe studies the intersection of emotional and cognitive health, drawing on neuroscience, neuropsychology, and clinical psychology. Her work focuses on reward processing, positive affect, well-being, and the ways these processes change with aging and depression.

She uses complementary EEG and fMRI methods to investigate neural mechanisms linking depression and cognitive decline in older adults. Her broader goal is to inform interventions that support mental and cognitive health in aging. She completed doctoral training in Clinical Psychology through the SDSU/UC San Diego joint program and neuropsychology/geropsychology fellowship training at the San Francisco VA.
summary: Studies reward processing, emotional well-being, depression, and cognitive health in aging using EEG, fMRI, and neuropsychology.

name: Carlos Daniel Carrasco
bio: Carlos Daniel Carrasco is a cognitive and computational neuroscientist studying attention, working memory, and decision-making with human EEG, fMRI, behavioral experiments, and multivariate methods. He investigates how the brain prioritizes rare and behaviorally relevant information and how neural signals may help identify risk for psychosis.

He earned his PhD in Neuroscience at UC Davis in 2024, working with Steven J. Luck at the Center for Mind and Brain. His research examined enhanced working-memory representations for rare events and showed how multivariate decoding can increase effect sizes across commonly studied ERP components.

At UCSF and the San Francisco VA, he works with Daniel Mathalon on large-scale EEG and fMRI data from AMP SCZ and NAPLS. His postdoctoral work includes P300 habituation, alpha event-related desynchronization, and PCA-based methods for isolating ERP signals. A recurring theme is improving the rigor, reproducibility, and clinical usefulness of human neuroscience data.
Outside research, he enjoys exploring the outdoors, playing guitar, and spending time with friends.
summary: Cognitive and computational neuroscientist studying attention, working memory, and psychosis-risk biomarkers with EEG, fMRI, and multivariate methods.

name: Maya Wong
academic: BIEEGL, UCSF / San Francisco VA · Clinical Cognitive Psychophysiology Lab, University of Minnesota
bio: Maya Wong is a joint postdoctoral fellow with the Brain Imaging and EEG Laboratory at UCSF and the San Francisco VA and Holly Hamilton’s Clinical Cognitive Psychophysiology Lab at the University of Minnesota. Her research interests include psychosis, minority stress, recovery, resilience, and the biosocial determinants of mental health.

Public VA and UCSF listings describe her work in clinical research and early psychosis, including assessment and therapy roles with the Path Program. This profile brings together those professional sources with her new lab listing.
summary: Joint postdoctoral fellow with BIEEGL and the University of Minnesota, studying psychosis, recovery, resilience, and mental health equity.

name: Wendy Torrens
bio: Wendy Alfonso Torrens is a neuroscientist studying sensory and cognitive processing in schizophrenia-related traits. Her work includes EEG methods and research on making electrophysiology more accessible across hair textures.

She earned her BA in Psychology at Colorado State University–Pueblo and her MS and PhD in Neuroscience at the University of Nevada, Reno. The Haigh Lab’s alumni page identifies her as a postdoctoral researcher at the UCSF VA working with Daniel Mathalon. Her work on the Universal Electroencephalography Clip addresses hair-texture bias in EEG recordings.
summary: Studies sensory and cognitive processing and develops more inclusive EEG methods, including work addressing hair-texture bias.

name: Holly Hamilton
bio: Holly Hamilton is an Assistant Professor of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences at the University of Minnesota and a staff psychologist and clinician investigator at the Minneapolis VA Health Care System. She directs the Clinical Cognitive Psychophysiology Lab.

Her research combines electrophysiology, neuroimaging, behavioral tasks, and clinical assessment to understand cognitive mechanisms in schizophrenia and other serious mental illnesses. She also investigates biological and clinical factors associated with vulnerability and resilience to psychosis, with the goal of informing early identification and intervention.

Hamilton earned her PhD in Clinical Psychology at UCLA and her BA in Psychology and Art History at New York University. She completed internship and postdoctoral training at the San Francisco VA and UCSF, where she was a faculty member before moving to Minnesota.
summary: Investigates cognitive mechanisms, psychosis risk, and resilience using EEG, neuroimaging, behavioral tasks, and clinical assessment.

bio: Brian Roach is a consultant to the lab and a longtime contributor to EEG and multimodal neuroscience research. His coauthored studies include work on neural–hemodynamic coupling, sensory prediction, and brain connectivity in schizophrenia and psychosis.
